strengths: The paper makes a useful Algorithms/General contribution by showing that averaging log-likelihoods across token orders substantially improves generative classification with an existing any-order AR model. The method is simple, requires no discriminative fine-tuning, and addresses a relevant limitation of fixed-order classifiers.

The controlled raster-versus-random comparison supports the central empirical finding. In Table 1, increasing K from 1 to 20 improves ImageNet accuracy from 67.0% to 76.9%, exceeding the raster model's 70.1%, with substantial improvements on ImageNet-R and Sketch.

The larger model produces compelling results against diffusion classifiers: Table 2 reports 81.3% versus 77.2% for DiT on ImageNet, 53.0% versus 40.2% on ImageNet-R, and 45.9% versus 36.7% on Sketch. Figure 6 additionally demonstrates a favorable accuracy–runtime tradeoff using actual single-A100 measurements.

The experimental investigation is reasonably broad, including multiple generative baselines, two model sizes, retrained DINOv2 comparisons, tokenizer and aggregation ablations, diffusion weighting experiments, and real-world distribution shifts. The substantial Camelyon17 OOD gains provide evidence beyond ImageNet variants.

The paper clearly acknowledges that its practical score is a lower bound rather than the marginalized likelihood itself, and Table 5 directly compares these alternatives. Overall, the empirical contribution supports acceptance despite the limitations below.
weaknesses: The proposed explanation that order averaging captures more comprehensive semantic information remains suggestive. Figures 3–5 demonstrate changing token contributions and improved accuracy, but do not distinguish this explanation from ordinary ensemble variance reduction. A compute-matched fixed-order ensemble or augmentation baseline would strengthen the mechanistic claim; evidence currently comes from one any-order architecture.

Several claims overstate the consistency of the improvements. Contrary to Section 5's statement that random orders with K>1 outperform raster ordering across all validation sets, Table 1 shows lower ImageNet-A accuracy even at K=20 (14.6% versus 17.4%). Table 6 also shows DiT slightly outperforming RandAR on FMoW. These exceptions should inform the conclusions about ordering and robustness.

Important reproducibility details are missing or contradictory. Section 6.6 specifies MaskGIT for WILDS, whereas Appendix A specifies LlamaGen with noise augmentation. The training noise level or sampling distribution is not specified, and the promised code/model link is blank. These issues particularly hinder reproduction of the tokenizer-dependent and WILDS findings.

Statistical support is limited for smaller differences. Several ImageNet evaluations use only 2,000 images without confidence intervals or repeated permutation estimates, while the three-seed WILDS results omit dispersion. Large XL-model gains are persuasive, but claims based on small margins—such as RandAR-L versus DiT on ImageNet—need more qualification.

The efficiency advantage is credible, but the precise 25× claim is difficult to reproduce from Figure 6 alone: operating-point settings, batching, precision, and timing boundaries are not fully documented. Classification still requires scoring many class–order combinations and takes seconds per image, limiting practical competitiveness with discriminative classifiers despite comparable accuracy.

Two technical statements need correction or qualification: Equation 2 omits the negative sign relating denoising error to the ELBO, and Table 5 compares finite-sample estimators, so it does not establish that the exact marginalized-likelihood classifier is intrinsically inferior. Neither issue invalidates the observed classification gains.

strengths: The paper makes a useful Algorithms/General contribution by showing that averaging class-conditional log-likelihoods across token orders substantially improves generative image classification with an existing any-order AR model. The method is simple and does not require discriminative fine-tuning.

The controlled raster-versus-random-order experiment supports the central empirical claim. In Table 1, increasing K from 1 to 20 improves ImageNet accuracy from 67.0% to 76.9%, exceeding the raster model’s 70.1%, with substantial improvements on ImageNet-R and Sketch.

The main comparisons show meaningful gains over diffusion classifiers. RandAR-XL achieves 81.3% versus DiT-XL’s 77.2% on ImageNet, 53.0% versus 40.2% on ImageNet-R, and 45.9% versus 36.7% on Sketch. Figure 6 reports measured A100 runtimes and supports a substantially better accuracy–latency tradeoff.

The experimental coverage is substantial: multiple model sizes, several generative baselines, an ImageNet-trained DINOv2 comparison, tokenizer and aggregation ablations, diffusion weighting controls, and distribution-shift datasets. The particularly large Camelyon17 OOD gains provide evidence beyond ImageNet.

Equation 5 correctly distinguishes the marginalized likelihood from its expected-log-likelihood lower bound, and Table 5 directly tests this consequential design choice. Overall, the empirical contribution supports a slight preference for acceptance despite the reservations below.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited: the central operation is log-likelihood averaging using the existing RandAR architecture. The proposed explanation—that averaging captures broader semantic information—is plausible but not established by the qualitative heatmaps. These use clipped differences against a randomly chosen incorrect class, and no compute-matched raster ensemble or augmentation-averaging control isolates order diversity from more general ensemble benefits.

Several claims overstate the results. Section 5 says random orders with K>1 outperform raster order across all validation sets, but Table 1 shows lower ImageNet-A accuracy even at K=20: 14.6% versus 17.4%. The abstract’s consistent superiority over diffusion classifiers also needs qualification: Table 6 shows slightly lower FMoW accuracy and essentially tied results in some other settings.

Important reproducibility details are unresolved. Section 6.6 specifies the MaskGIT tokenizer for the distribution-shift experiments, whereas Appendix A specifies LlamaGen with noise augmentation. This is consequential because Section 6.4 establishes tokenizer sensitivity. The training noise-level distribution is also unspecified, and the abstract’s promised code/model link is blank.

Uncertainty is inadequately quantified. Several ImageNet results use only 2,000 images, without confidence intervals, repeated subset evaluations, or reported variability from sampled token orders. The statement that larger subsets give only minor changes is not supported numerically. This particularly weakens interpretation of small gains, such as RandAR-L’s 78.0% versus DiT-L’s 77.1%. Table 6 also omits variability despite discussing multiple training seeds.

The comparison claims need more precise scope. DINOv2 is retrained on ImageNet1K, so these results demonstrate competitiveness with that controlled baseline rather than with released large-data SSL models generally. Likewise, the reported 25× speedup should identify the exact operating points, batching, and numerical precision. Classification still takes seconds to tens of seconds per image and scales with the number of candidate classes, limiting practical competitiveness with discriminative classifiers.

strengths: The paper makes a useful empirical and methodological contribution to generative image classification: averaging log-likelihoods across token orders substantially improves an existing any-order autoregressive model without discriminative fine-tuning. Although technically simple, the approach challenges the apparent superiority of diffusion classifiers.

The central ablation is convincing. In Table 1, increasing K from 1 to 20 improves ImageNet accuracy from 67.0% to 76.9%, ImageNet-R from 35.1% to 46.9%, and ImageNet-Sketch from 28.9% to 40.9%. The separately trained raster-order control helps isolate the benefit of supporting multiple orders.

The main comparisons show meaningful gains. RandAR-XL achieves 81.3% ImageNet accuracy versus 77.2% for DiT, with larger improvements on several distribution-shift benchmarks. It also compares favorably with the ImageNet-trained DINOv2 baseline on renditions, sketches, and Gaussian corruption, while transparently reporting weaker ImageNet-A performance.

The evaluation extends beyond standard ImageNet classification and includes useful tokenizer, likelihood-aggregation, diffusion-weighting, and noise-averaging ablations. The large Camelyon17 OOD gains are particularly encouraging. Actual A100 timing curves provide stronger efficiency evidence than forward-pass counts alone.
weaknesses: The mechanistic interpretation is less established than the accuracy gains. Averaged heatmaps against one randomly chosen incorrect class do not demonstrate that the method systematically captures more complete object structure. A compute-matched raster-model ensemble or augmentation baseline would help distinguish order-specific benefits from general ensembling effects. The contribution is primarily a successful inference strategy and empirical finding, since the any-order architecture itself comes from RandAR.

Some robustness claims exceed the evidence. Contrary to the statement following Table 1, random-order averaging does not outperform raster ordering on every benchmark: ImageNet-A accuracy is 14.6% at K=20 versus 17.4% for raster ordering. Table 6 also shows slightly worse FMoW performance than DiT. These exceptions should qualify claims of consistent superiority. ImageNet-C coverage is limited to two corruptions at one severity.

Statistical support is insufficient for the smaller improvements. Several principal benchmarks use only 2,000 images, without confidence intervals, paired significance analysis, or quantified subset sensitivity. For example, the 0.9-point RandAR-L advantage over DiT on ImageNet is difficult to assess. WILDS results mention averaging three seeds but omit dispersion, and the scope of this repetition across model families is unclear.

Important implementation details are inconsistent or missing. Section 6.6 specifies MaskGIT for WILDS, whereas Appendix A specifies LlamaGen with noise augmentation. The augmentation's noise-level distribution is not specified. Runtime results omit batching and numerical-precision details and do not identify the exact operating points yielding the headline 25-fold speedup. The promised code/model link is also absent from the supplied manuscript.

The probabilistic terminology needs tightening. Equation 5 correctly derives a lower bound, but subsequent passages describe its average-log-likelihood score as the marginalized log-likelihood itself; Table 5 demonstrates that these are materially different classifiers. Equation 2 also omits the negative sign required when relating denoising squared error to an ELBO. These are correctable presentation issues, but precision matters because likelihood estimation is central to the method.

strengths: The paper makes a useful empirical contribution to generative image classification: averaging log-likelihoods across token orders substantially improves any-order autoregressive classifiers without discriminative fine-tuning. The matched raster/random-order experiment isolates an important design choice, and Table 5 clearly supports averaging log-likelihoods over averaging likelihoods.

The main results are strong. RandAR-XL achieves 81.3% ImageNet accuracy versus 77.2% for DiT-XL, with larger improvements on ImageNet-R and Sketch. Figure 6 demonstrates a favorable accuracy–runtime trade-off using measured A100 runtimes rather than forward-pass counts alone.

The evaluation is unusually broad, covering several generative model families, DINOv2 linear probing, real-world distribution shifts, alternative tokenizers, another order-conditioned architecture, and masked-diffusion scoring. The supplementary diffusion-weighting and few-step-model experiments strengthen the baseline comparisons.

The analysis provides useful insights beyond benchmark performance. The token-prefix experiments, likelihood-aggregation ablation, and AR-versus-masked-diffusion evaluation help explain which scoring choices matter. The substantial Camelyon17 improvements also suggest value beyond conventional ImageNet classification.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is relatively modest: the method applies an existing any-order model and a standard Monte Carlo average of its training objective. Its strongest contribution is the empirical demonstration. The stronger interpretation that order averaging produces more comprehensive object understanding remains suggestive: clipped likelihood differences against one random incorrect class and selected visualizations do not distinguish this explanation from ordinary ensemble variance reduction.

Some central claims exceed the evidence. Section 5 says random-order scoring with K>1 surpasses raster scoring across all validation sets, but Table 1 shows worse ImageNet-A accuracy even at K=20 (14.6% versus 17.4%). Diffusion superiority is also not universal: DiT slightly leads on FMoW and on CelebA worst-group accuracy at B scale. These exceptions should qualify the abstract and conclusions.

The claimed exact equivalence to masked diffusion in Appendix D needs correction and additional assumptions. Equation 6 introduces a factor 1/N absent from the sequence log-likelihood, leaves the mask distribution unspecified, and replaces an ordered causal prefix with an unordered observed set without explaining how RandAR's dependence on prefix ordering is handled. This does not invalidate the main classifier, but the theoretical claim is not established as written. Likewise, the practical score in Equation 5 is a lower-bound estimate, not the marginalized log-likelihood itself.

Several reported differences lack adequate uncertainty estimates. ImageNet-Val, Sketch, and corruption results use only 2,000 images, making small gains—such as the L-scale ImageNet improvement over DiT—difficult to assess without paired confidence intervals. Training-seed variability for the generative models is also unclear, particularly for the real-world shift experiments. The large improvements are more convincing than the near-ties.

Reproducibility and the scope of the efficiency comparison need clarification. The manuscript omits the latent-noise sampling settings, subset identities, detailed DINOv2 probing configuration, and inference batching/precision underlying the 25× claim; the promised code/model URL is absent. RandAR still requires class-dependent evaluation and seconds per image, so competitiveness with DINOv2 concerns accuracy rather than practical inference efficiency. These limitations should accompany the headline comparison.

strengths: Evaluated as Algorithms/General, the paper makes a useful empirical contribution: averaging log-likelihoods across token orders substantially improves generative classification with existing any-order AR models, without discriminative fine-tuning.

The gains over diffusion classifiers are substantial, particularly at XL scale. Table 2 reports 81.3% versus 77.2% ImageNet accuracy for RandAR and DiT, with larger improvements on ImageNet-R, Sketch, and Gaussian corruption. Figure 6 supports a favorable accuracy–runtime trade-off using measured A100 runtimes.

The experimental investigation is unusually broad: controlled raster-versus-random training, order-count and likelihood-aggregation ablations, tokenizer experiments, an additional RAR architecture, masked-diffusion evaluation, and several real-world distribution shifts. These provide evidence beyond a single favorable benchmark.

The comparisons include meaningful alternatives such as DINOv2, A-VARC+, representation-aligned diffusion models, and few-step MeanFlow. The supplementary evaluations address several plausible competing explanations and show where discriminative models remain stronger.
The central empirical result supports acceptance despite the modest algorithmic novelty and qualifications below.
weaknesses: The mechanistic explanation is less established than the performance improvement. Clipped likelihood differences against a randomly selected incorrect class and qualitative heatmaps do not demonstrate that order averaging causes greater shape sensitivity or reduced shortcut reliance. Controlled shape/texture or background interventions would strengthen this interpretation.

Several claims overstate consistency. Section 5 says random-order models with K>1 outperform raster order across all validation sets, but Table 1 shows lower ImageNet-A accuracy even at K=20 (14.6% versus 17.4%). Table 7 also shows RandAR slightly trailing DiT on FMoW. These exceptions should qualify the broad robustness claims.

Statistical reporting limits interpretation of smaller improvements. Several ImageNet results use only 2,000 images, without confidence intervals or variability across subset selection and sampled orders. The statement that larger subsets produce only minor changes is not supported quantitatively. These omissions matter more for small differences than for the larger reported gains.

The theoretical presentation needs correction. Equation 2 writes the diffusion ELBO as a positive denoising error, omitting the negative sign and relevant constants. Appendix D introduces a factor of 1/N inconsistent with the full log-likelihood and leaves the mask distribution and treatment of ordered prefixes insufficiently specified. These issues weaken the claimed exact equivalence, although they do not invalidate the main classification experiments.

The implemented score is an average log-likelihood, a lower bound on the log of the order-mixture likelihood, rather than the marginalized likelihood itself. Table 5 usefully establishes that this distinction matters empirically, but subsequent descriptions sometimes conflate the two. The methodological novelty should be framed as an effective scoring strategy built on existing any-order modeling.

Reproducibility and practical efficiency reporting remain incomplete. The supplied manuscript has no visible code/model URL after its availability statement, and does not fully specify the noise-augmentation distribution, evaluation subset selection, or timing batch configuration. The 25× claim should identify its exact comparison point; classification still takes seconds per image and scales with the number of candidate classes.

strengths: The paper makes a useful Algorithms/General contribution by showing that averaging class-conditional log-likelihoods across token orders substantially improves visual autoregressive classification. The method is simple, requires no discriminative fine-tuning, and addresses a meaningful limitation of existing generative classifiers.

The central empirical result is convincing. In Table 2, RandAR-XL achieves 81.3% ImageNet accuracy versus 77.2% for DiT-XL, with larger gains on ImageNet-R (53.0% versus 40.2%) and Sketch (45.9% versus 36.7%). The controlled raster/random-order comparison and the gains as K increases directly support the proposed approach.

The evaluation is unusually broad: it includes multiple generative and discriminative baselines, tokenizer and aggregation ablations, another order-conditioned architecture, masked-diffusion scoring, and real-world distribution shifts. The supplementary comparisons with diffusion weighting strategies, additional noise averaging, and few-step models strengthen the baseline evaluation.

Measured accuracy–runtime curves on an A100 support a substantial efficiency advantage over diffusion classifiers. The strong Camelyon17 OOD results and competitive performance against ImageNet-trained DINOv2 also make the findings relevant beyond a narrow in-domain benchmark.
weaknesses: The probabilistic interpretation needs greater precision. The implemented score averages log-likelihoods, rather than computing the logarithm of the order-marginalized likelihood; Table 5 establishes that this surrogate works better, but does not explain why. Appendix D also inserts a factor of 1/N into an equality with the full sequence log-likelihood and replaces ordered prefixes with unordered observed sets without explaining how RandAR's dependence on prefix order is handled. The masked-diffusion equivalence therefore needs corrected normalization and explicit assumptions. These issues weaken the theoretical explanation, rather than the observed classification gains.

Several claims are broader than the results. Section 5 says random-order models with K>1 outperform the raster model across all validation sets, but Table 1 shows lower ImageNet-A accuracy even at K=20 (14.6% versus 17.4%). Table 7 likewise shows that RandAR does not consistently beat DiT on FMoW. Comparisons with 'state-of-the-art SSL' should explicitly refer to the paper's ImageNet1K-trained DINOv2 configurations; RandAR also trails these models substantially on ImageNet-A and ObjectNet.

Uncertainty reporting is limited. Several main benchmarks use only 2,000 images, and confidence intervals or repeated permutation-sampling results are absent. The assertion that larger subsets produce only minor changes is not quantified. This particularly affects interpretation of smaller differences, such as the 0.9-point improvement over DiT-L on ImageNet. For the real-world experiments, the scope of the three-seed averaging should be clarified and variability reported.

The proposed mechanism remains suggestive. Heatmaps based on clipped likelihood differences against a randomly chosen incorrect class can illustrate spatial evidence, but do not establish that averaging improves shape understanding or reduces shortcut reliance. Quantitative foreground/background or cue-conflict evaluations would strengthen this interpretation; the current evidence more directly establishes the benefit of averaging predictions across orders.

Reproducibility and practical efficiency reporting need additional detail. The manuscript does not specify the training distribution or strength of latent-noise augmentation, and runtime measurements omit batching, precision, memory use, and the exact operating points supporting the 25× claim. The abstract's code-and-model availability statement has no link. Inference still takes seconds to minutes per image, so the demonstrated speed advantage is primarily relative to diffusion classifiers.
